title: Assumed 1 ms relative timing variation raised the minimum model residual in 57 selected Allen mouse input pairs
abstract: We tested a model of convergent excitation and inhibition with fixed gain and trial-to-trial timing variation. We used passed current-clamp fits from the same -55 mV holding bin in Allen Synaptic Physiology r2.1. The selected mouse visual-cortex sample had 57 input pairs at 47 targets from 43 inferred donors. We optimized mean relative delay and one inhibitory gain for each pair. Gaussian relative-delay variation with a standard deviation of 1 ms increased mean residual energy from 0.2641 to 0.2919 of excitatory-input energy. The increase was 0.0279, with a conditional 95% donor bootstrap interval of 0.0194 to 0.0373. Distance and interior-fit checks kept the increase above a chosen 0.01 reporting threshold. Gaussian timing variation cannot improve this optimized expected-energy score under the stated model; the data set its size. Timing variation was assumed, not measured. Linear voltage addition, fixed kernels, inferred donors, missing fits and selected slice circuits limit the result. This extends a published finite-rise benchmark in the same cohort. It is not independent biological validation.

display.caption: Assumed relative-delay variation raises the minimum expected energy residual in the selected mouse model. Left: equal-donor means. Right: donor penalties at 1 ms standard deviation. The 0.01 line is a chosen reporting threshold, not a measured physiological standard.

citations.reason: Reuses the published fit extract and code for response rates, overlap, donor labels and hierarchy. Adds random relative delay, fixed-gain expected energy, and optimal mean delay.
